values: More than thirty years later, in seventeen oh-four, in London, Newton publishes a book called Opticks. And on page ninety, he gives his answer.
It's a sentence that's easy to read past. "For the rays to speak properly are not coloured." In plain words, strictly speaking, the rays have no colour.
All they have, he goes on, is "a certain power and disposition to stir up a sensation of this or that colour".

That sounds like it clashes with the prism. It doesn't. What's in sunlight is many kinds of ray. The light coming off that geranium isn't pink. Each ray only has a kind of push. And the pink is what happens when that push reaches whoever is looking.
So, on Newton's view, colour isn't really in the flower. It isn't in the light either. It's something that happens where the light meets a person.

But a geranium and a leaf still look different. Newton has an answer for that, too. In his letter from Cambridge, he says things get their colours by sending back some kinds of light more than others. A geranium sends back one mix. A leaf sends back another. Neither one is painting the light. Each is choosing from it.
That also explains the candle. Candlelight is much yellower than daylight, with far less blue in it. So by candle, the geranium has a different mix of rays to choose from.
And to most people, that change hardly matters. Their eyes still call it pink. Dalton's eyes don't.

Newton also gives us the rainbow we learn at school. He splits his band of colours into seven. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. And he spaces them in the same proportions as the seven steps of a musical scale.
Seven notes, seven colours. It's tidy. Possibly a little too tidy. People have been arguing about indigo ever since.
Here's why all this matters for Dalton. He knows this science. He says he's "pretty well acquainted with the theory of light and colours". And on Newton's terms, his idea makes good sense.
Colour is what happens when certain rays reach the back of the eye. So a tinted jelly in front of it changes which rays arrive. Change the rays, and you change the colour.
But a guess about the inside of an eye can only be tested one way. Someone has to open it.
